column2: A mineral soil horizon near the surface, usually darkened by organic matter mixed with mineral particles.
Wearing away of rock by sediment carried against it by water, wind or ice; also called corrasion.
The surface layer above permafrost that thaws seasonally and freezes again.
Cooling as an air parcel expands when pressure falls, without exchanging heat with its surroundings. Rising air commonly cools this way.
Köppen tropical rainforest climate: every month averages at least 18 °C and receives at least 60 mm of precipitation.
A large body of air with broadly similar temperature and moisture characteristics acquired over a source region.
A fold with the oldest rocks in its core. In a simple upright anticline, the layers arch upwards and dip away from the centre; overturned folds can have different geometry.
An ancient mountain belt in eastern North America, assembled through several Palaeozoic collisions during the closing of oceans and formation of Pangaea.
A layer of rock or sediment with low permeability that slows groundwater flow. It may confine an aquifer without being completely impermeable.
A narrow, sharp ridge formed where glaciers erode adjoining valleys or cirques. Striding Edge in the Lake District is an example.
An alternative spelling of arête: a sharp ridge separating glacially eroded valleys or cirques.
A mechanically weak part of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere. It is predominantly solid rock that deforms slowly over geological time.
A defined length of 149,597,870,700 m, approximately Earth's mean distance from the Sun; abbreviated au or AU.
The angle between a body's rotation axis and the perpendicular to its orbital plane. Earth's tilt is about 23.44°, and its axis keeps nearly the same direction over one orbit.
The main, usually steep section of a hillslope between its shoulder and footslope; material commonly moves through it downslope.
A crescent-shaped dune formed where sand supply is limited and wind mainly blows from one direction. Its horns extend downwind.
In a rain-shadow model, high ground that forces approaching air to rise; its height and orientation influence uplift.
An elongated sandy island lying roughly parallel to the coast, separated from the mainland by a lagoon or other shallow water.
A fine-grained volcanic rock rich in iron- and magnesium-bearing minerals. Basaltic magma is generally less viscous than silica-rich magma.
The sustained part of river discharge supplied mainly by groundwater and other delayed stores between rainfall events.
A stream whose former headwaters have been diverted into another drainage system by river capture.
A large ecological region characterised by its vegetation and associated organisms, influenced strongly by climate, soils and disturbance.
With your back to the wind in the Northern Hemisphere, lower pressure generally lies to your left; the relation reverses in the Southern Hemisphere. Surface friction modifies the angle.
Köppen hot desert climate: precipitation falls below the desert aridity threshold and mean annual temperature is at least 18 °C.
A large volcanic depression formed mainly when the ground collapses into an underlying magma reservoir after magma is withdrawn.
An ancient mountain belt formed during Palaeozoic continental collisions, now exposed in places including Scotland, Scandinavia and Greenland.
The earliest period of the Palaeozoic Era, beginning about 539 million years ago; its rocks record a major diversification of animal life.
Chemical weathering in which dissolved carbon dioxide forms weak carbonic acid that reacts with carbonate minerals such as calcite.
Köppen temperate oceanic climate, with no dry season and warm rather than hot summers. London is a familiar example.
A bowl-shaped hollow with steep sides at the head of a glacial valley, enlarged by ice erosion and weathering. A lake, called a tarn, may occupy it after the ice retreats.
The finest soil mineral particles, less than 0.002 mm across in the USDA system. Their large surface area strongly affects water and nutrient retention.
The statistical pattern of weather over a long period, commonly 30 years, including averages, seasonal variation and extremes.
The advancing boundary of a colder air mass that displaces warmer air. Uplift near the front can produce cloud and rain, with weather depending on moisture and stability.
A curved, comma-like cloud pattern often seen in satellite views of developing or mature extratropical cyclones.
A map projection that balances several kinds of distortion without preserving any one property exactly everywhere.
A passage through which magma and volcanic gases rise towards an eruptive vent.
A saturated permeable layer bounded above by a low-permeability layer. Water in a well rises to its pressure level, which may or may not reach the ground surface.
The gently sloping, submerged outer part of a continent, extending from the coast to the shelf break.
A simplified description of interconnected deep and surface ocean circulation. Real flow involves branching currents, mixing, winds and density differences.

An apparent acceleration in a rotating reference frame. For horizontal motion on Earth it deflects flow right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern; that horizontal component vanishes at the equator.
The highest part of a hill or ridge. Soil thickness and drainage there depend on the local relief, geology and climate.
Earth's outermost compositional layer of solid rock. Oceanic crust averages about 7 km thick; continental crust commonly spans roughly 30–70 km.
The temperature above which a ferromagnetic mineral loses its spontaneous magnetisation. Cooling minerals can acquire a record of Earth's field near their magnetic blocking temperatures.
A circulation around a low-pressure centre: anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern. Tropical and extratropical cyclones form through different processes.
Changes to a river's discharge timing and magnitude caused by storing and releasing water from a reservoir.
The immense timespan of geological history, extending back about 4.54 billion years to Earth's formation.
A body of sediment built where a river enters a sea or lake and deposits enough material to accumulate. Distributary channels often cross its surface.
Mass divided by volume, measured in kg m⁻³. In most ocean conditions, cooling or increasing salinity makes seawater denser.
In meteorology, a region of low atmospheric pressure; in UK usage, commonly an extratropical cyclone.
A teaching description for waves that tend to remove sediment from a beach, with strong backwash relative to swash. Net change also depends on sediment and wave conditions.
The volume of water passing a river cross-section per unit time, usually measured in m³ s⁻¹. For mean velocity v and cross-sectional area A, Q = Av.
A change in area, shape, distance or direction caused by projecting a curved surface onto a plane. No flat world map preserves all of them everywhere.
A closed depression in karst terrain, formed by dissolution or collapse of soluble rock. Also called a sinkhole; some drain underground and others hold water.

A lowering of water level. In the tsunami lab it means the withdrawal of the sea before some waves; many tsunami arrive without this warning. Groundwater drawdown means a lowered water table or pressure level.
An elongated hill streamlined beneath moving ice, commonly made of glacial sediment and sometimes containing bedrock. Its long axis usually follows former ice flow.
A grid coordinate measuring distance east from a defined origin. Read eastings before northings in a grid reference.
The warm phase of ENSO, marked by unusually warm sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific and coupled atmospheric changes.
The instant when the Sun crosses Earth's equatorial plane. Daylight is close to twelve hours around this date, but the Sun's disc, refraction and latitude affect observed day length.
The wearing away and removal of material by moving water, wind, ice or gravity. Weathering breaks down material in place.
A partly enclosed coastal water body where freshwater meets and mixes with seawater, influenced by tides.
Describing a change in global mean sea level, for example from changing ocean-water volume or ocean-basin capacity.
Outside the tropics. An extratropical cyclone is a storm system usually associated with fronts and horizontal temperature contrasts.
An offset origin used to keep map-grid coordinates convenient and usually positive. The British National Grid uses one southwest of Great Britain.
Carbon exchanges among the atmosphere, living organisms, soils and upper ocean over relatively short timescales, from days to centuries.
The mean midlatitude atmospheric circulation, with poleward near-surface flow and equatorward flow aloft. It is an indirect cell maintained largely by weather systems.
Relatively flat land beside a river that is shaped by channel migration and flood deposition and may be inundated when the river overflows.
A rate of transfer of a quantity such as water, carbon or energy; some uses express that rate per unit area.
Coal, oil or natural gas formed from ancient organic material. Burning it transfers carbon from long-term geological stores to the atmosphere.
A long seafloor feature extending beyond a ridge-offset transform fault. Beyond the active transform segment, both sides move with the same plate.
Rock breakdown associated with freezing water and ice growth in cracks. Repeated freezing, thawing and ice segregation can widen the fractures.
The generation of Earth's magnetic field by motion of electrically conducting liquid metal in the outer core, influenced by Earth's rotation.
Soil features associated with prolonged saturation and oxygen shortage, often including grey colours and rusty mottles from changes in iron chemistry.
The part of a sundial that casts a shadow. For a vertical gnomon on level ground, shadow length depends on its height and the Sun's altitude.
Tapered strips of a map designed to be fitted around a globe; small strips reduce the distortion needed to cover a sphere.
Warming of a planet's surface and lower atmosphere because gases and clouds absorb and emit thermal infrared radiation, affecting the loss of energy to space.
An area identified by a map grid. In British National Grid notation, four, six and eight figures identify 1 km, 100 m and 10 m squares respectively.
A fast, warm western-boundary current in the North Atlantic, flowing from the Florida Straits along the eastern United States before turning offshore.
A submerged seamount with a relatively flat summit, commonly formed when a volcanic island is eroded near sea level and later subsides.
A sharp pyramidal mountain peak formed by erosion from glaciers on several sides; the Matterhorn is a well-known example.
A region of persistent volcanism that can occur within a plate or at a boundary. Many hotspots are associated with mantle upwelling; not all have an established deep plume origin.
A graph showing how river discharge or water level changes with time. A storm hydrograph may be shown alongside a separate rainfall graph to compare timing and response.
Uranus or Neptune: a giant planet with a hydrogen–helium atmosphere and an interior enriched in substances such as water, ammonia and methane. These are not simply layers of ordinary frozen ice.
A wedge of ground ice formed as water enters thermal-contraction cracks and freezes repeatedly in permafrost.
The angle between incoming radiation and the surface normal. A larger incidence angle spreads the same beam over more ground; solar altitude is measured above the horizon instead.
The strength of earthquake shaking and its effects at a particular place. It depends on the earthquake, distance, local ground and built structures.
In structural geology, the uplift and shortening of a previously subsiding basin. A temperature inversion in meteorology is a different use of the word.
The intertropical convergence zone: a shifting belt where tropical trade winds meet and moist air often rises. Its position varies with season, oceans and land heating.
The Cretaceous–Palaeogene boundary, about 66 million years ago, marking a major mass extinction associated with the Chicxulub impact and wider environmental change.
A thousand years. Used with an age reference to express geological dates, for example 20 ka before present.
For bodies orbiting the same dominant mass, orbital period squared is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis: T² ∝ a³.
The cool phase of ENSO, with unusually cool central and eastern equatorial Pacific surface waters and associated changes in tropical winds and rainfall.
The delay between a rainfall reference, commonly peak rainfall, and peak river discharge. State the convention used when reading a storm hydrograph.
A local wind from land towards the sea, commonly at night when land has cooled faster. Larger-scale winds can weaken or prevent it.
The side sheltered from the prevailing wind. Descending air there often warms and has lower relative humidity.
A raised bank beside a river, either built naturally by overbank sediment deposition or constructed to reduce flooding. Also written levee.
A raised bank beside a river, either built naturally by overbank sediment deposition or constructed to reduce flooding. Also written levée.
The distance light travels in a vacuum in one Julian year: about 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m. It is a length, not a duration.
A USDA soil-texture class containing a mixture of sand, silt and clay; loam is not defined as equal thirds of the three fractions.
Stars in the Sun's neighbourhood, at distances usually expressed in light years or parsecs. The nearest star system is Alpha Centauri.
A spiral whose radius grows exponentially with angle. A geological-time display can use such a layout, but its labels must state how time is mapped to distance.
An eclipse occurring when the Moon passes through Earth's shadow near full Moon and an orbital node. It can be penumbral, partial or total.
A million years. Often used for geological ages, such as 66 Ma; Myr commonly denotes a duration of a million years.
Partly or wholly molten rock beneath the surface, often containing crystals and dissolved gases. Molten rock erupted at the surface is called lava.
An upwelling of unusually hot mantle material that may supply hotspot volcanism. It is mostly deforming solid rock, with partial melting possible near the top.
A bend in a river channel. Outer-bank erosion and inner-bank deposition commonly move the bend across a floodplain; a cutoff can leave an oxbow lake.
A large, low-angle thrust fault at a subduction boundary. Sudden slip on its shallow offshore part can displace the seafloor and generate a tsunami.
The atmospheric layer roughly 50–85 km above the surface, in which temperature generally falls with altitude. Many meteors become luminous here.
A submarine mountain system at a spreading boundary, where mantle upwelling and melting form new oceanic crust. Seafloor generally becomes older away from the spreading axis.
An extratropical low-pressure system that develops from contrasts in temperature and is commonly associated with warm and cold fronts.
A stream smaller than the valley it occupies, sometimes following river capture or the loss of former glacial meltwater discharge.
A USDA soil order characterised by a dark, base-rich surface horizon, often formed beneath grassland. It is not an exact synonym for every chernozem classification.
An accumulation of debris transported or deposited by a glacier, including lateral, medial, terminal and ground moraines.
A landform with substantial elevation and relief relative to its surroundings. There is no single globally accepted height separating mountains from hills.
North Atlantic Deep Water: a group of deep water masses formed through cooling, mixing and sinking in the North Atlantic and neighbouring seas.
The hemisphere of the Moon that usually faces Earth because the Moon rotates once per orbit. Libration lets us see somewhat more than half its surface over time.
Weathering, meltwater movement and other processes around persistent snow patches that can help enlarge shallow hollows.
A scale step of a factor of ten. Quantities differing by three orders of magnitude differ by roughly a factor of one thousand.
Ordnance Survey Great Britain. OSGB36 is a geodetic datum used with the British National Grid; it differs from the global WGS84 reference system.
Earth's liquid metallic layer, mainly iron with nickel and lighter elements, between about 2,890 and 5,150 km depth. It does not transmit shear waves.
A curved former meander channel separated from the main river. It may contain an oxbow lake or gradually fill with sediment.
A lake occupying a meander loop cut off from the main river channel, usually on a floodplain.
A compressional seismic wave with particle motion parallel to its travel direction. It travels through solids and liquids and is the faster body-wave type.
The distance at which one astronomical unit subtends one arcsecond; about 3.26 light years, or 3.086 × 10¹⁶ m.
Repeated ground patterns such as polygons, circles or stripes, produced by processes including frost sorting and thermal contraction in cold environments.
The greatest rate of river flow during a specified event or period, measured in m³ s⁻¹.
The part of a shadow where the light source is only partly obscured. On the Moon it produces subtler dimming than the umbra.
Ground that remains at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years. It may contain ice but need not be permanently ice-filled.
Pressure-gradient force: the force per unit mass associated with a pressure difference, directed from higher towards lower pressure.
The visible layer of the Sun from which most of its observed light escapes. Sunspots are relatively cooler, magnetically active regions within it.
The use of light energy to build organic molecules from carbon dioxide and water. Oxygen-producing photosynthesis transfers carbon into living matter.
A collection of particles orbiting a planet, ranging from fine dust to larger fragments. Saturn's rings consist mainly of water ice.
Describing a river regime mainly controlled by rainfall; its discharge seasonality reflects rainfall and catchment storage.
The pressure of water or gas within pores in soil or rock. Increasing water pressure can reduce effective stress and resistance to slope failure.
A number written as 10 raised to an exponent, used to express large or small quantities and compare their scales.
The informal span of Earth history before the Cambrian Period, covering the Hadean, Archaean and Proterozoic eons.
A difference in pressure between two places. It creates a pressure-gradient force that can start air moving.
The chosen zero of longitude. The modern reference meridian used by WGS84 lies about 102 m east of the historic Greenwich transit circle.
A former beach now above present sea level because of land uplift, a fall in sea level, or both.
A traditional soil term for a shallow, often acidic soil over hard, non-calcareous rock; commonly found on steep or exposed ground.
The characteristic seasonal pattern of river discharge, influenced by rainfall, snowmelt, storage and human regulation.
The variation in elevation within an area, often expressed as the difference between its highest and lowest points.
The typical time material remains in a store. For a well-mixed store at steady state, mean residence time is its amount divided by its outflow rate.
Processes that release energy from organic matter. Aerobic respiration consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and water.
A path of constant compass bearing, shown as a straight line on a Mercator map. Except for special cases, it is not the shortest path on a sphere.
An elongated region where the lithosphere is extending and thinning. Some continental rifts develop into ocean basins; others cease spreading.
The maximum elevation reached by a wave above a specified reference sea level as it moves onto land; distinct from inland inundation distance.
A shear seismic wave with particle motion perpendicular to its travel direction. It propagates through solids but not through the liquid outer core.
A five-category hurricane scale based on maximum sustained wind speed. It does not rate rainfall, storm surge or the full impact of a cyclone.
Transport in short hops or bounces, especially of sand grains moved by wind or flowing water.
Soil mineral particles 0.05–2 mm across in the USDA system. Other sediment classifications use a slightly different lower boundary.
A change between views representing very different sizes or distances. Each view needs its own scale because a single display cannot resolve all of them.
An underwater mountain, usually volcanic. Seamounts need not lie on an age-progressive hotspot chain or have once stood above sea level.
A tidal pattern with two high waters and two low waters in each lunar day, which averages about 24 hours 50 minutes.
Comparison of continental margins, rather than modern coastlines, when reconstructing former continental positions. Sediment cover and deformation make the fit approximate.
A broad volcano with gentle slopes built mainly by fluid lava flows, commonly basaltic. Mauna Loa is a classic example.
The change in a wave as it enters shallower water: it slows, its wavelength shortens, and its height may increase before breaking.
Soil mineral particles 0.002–0.05 mm across in the USDA system, intermediate between clay and sand.
Carbon transfer through rocks, sediments and the deep Earth, involving weathering, burial, metamorphism and volcanism over geological timescales.
Total solar irradiance near Earth's mean orbital distance, about 1,361 W m⁻² on a surface perpendicular to the rays above the atmosphere. It varies slightly over time.
An eclipse near new Moon when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun close to an orbital node. The apparent sizes determine whether it is total, annular or partial.
An elongated deposit of sand or shingle attached to land at one end and extending into water, commonly built by longshore sediment transport.
An isolated pillar of coastal rock left by erosion and cliff retreat, sometimes after the collapse of a sea arch. Old Harry is chalk; Durdle Door is an arch in limestone.
Flooding described by the water level after short-period surface waves are averaged out. Coastal still-water level can include the tide and storm surge.
A commonly steep-sided volcano built from successive lava flows and fragmental deposits. Its magma composition and eruption style can vary; many form above subduction zones.
Fault movement that is mainly horizontal and parallel to the fault's strike. Some strike-slip faults form plate-transform boundaries; others lie within plates.
The descent of one lithospheric plate beneath another into the mantle at a convergent boundary, commonly involving oceanic lithosphere.
A relatively cool, dark region of the solar photosphere associated with strong magnetic fields.
Flow in the upper ocean, driven by winds and pressure gradients and modified by rotation, coastlines and mixing.
Transport of fine sediment within moving water or air, kept aloft by turbulence rather than continuously resting on the bed or ground.
An opening where a surface stream enters underground drainage, usually in karst. A doline or sinkhole is a depression and need not contain a sinking stream.
A fold with the youngest rocks in its core. In a simple upright syncline, layers dip towards the centre; erosion can leave either a ridge or valley above it.
A statistical relationship between climate or weather variations in distant regions, such as the influence of ENSO on rainfall probabilities.
The boundary between the illuminated and dark hemispheres of a planet or moon. Earth's rotation carries places across it; changing solar declination alters its seasonal orientation.
The boundary between Earth's illuminated and dark hemispheres. Its position changes with time of day and with the Sun's seasonal declination.
A body of crust with a geological history distinct from neighbouring regions, often joined to a continent by tectonic accretion.
A belt of the highest mean temperatures at a given season. It shifts with seasonal heating and geography and does not always coincide with the geographic equator or ITCZ.
Relating to seawater density differences caused by temperature and salinity. These contribute to ocean overturning alongside wind forcing and mixing.
The very thin atmospheric layer above roughly 85 km where kinetic temperature generally rises with altitude as gases absorb energetic solar radiation. Much auroral activity occurs here.
An idealised elevation of the ocean surface in an equilibrium-tide model. Real tides are moving waves modified by basin shape, depth, rotation and coastlines.
Sediment deposited directly by glacier ice, usually containing an unsorted mixture of particle sizes.
A region using an agreed standard civil time. Boundaries follow political and practical choices and are not necessarily 15° wide.
A ridge of deposited sand or shingle connecting an island to the mainland or another island, often formed where wave refraction favours deposition.
A reference level above most atmospheric absorption and scattering, used when describing incoming and outgoing radiation. Solar irradiance also needs a specified distance and surface orientation.
A long, narrow depression in the seafloor associated with a subduction zone, where an oceanic plate bends down towards the mantle.
The boundary between the troposphere and stratosphere, identified mainly by a change in the vertical temperature gradient. Its altitude varies with latitude and weather.
The lowest atmospheric layer, containing most air mass and nearly all weather. It is typically about 8 km deep near the poles and 16–18 km near the tropics.
A view in which stated lengths use the same scale factor. If a display still exaggerates a feature or compresses distances, it must identify that exception explicitly.
The movement of deeper water towards the surface, often driven by winds that move surface water away or by large-scale ocean circulation.
An urban area that is warmer than nearby surroundings, often most evident at night. Surface materials, reduced evaporation, urban geometry and waste heat contribute.
A region of unusually warm tropical surface water. In the Pacific, its extent and position change with winds and ENSO.
In UK geography, the drainage divide separating basins. In US usage, watershed commonly means the entire drainage basin; check the context.
Physical breakdown or chemical alteration of rock at or near Earth's surface, without transporting the material away. Chemical weathering also participates in the carbon cycle.
A global geodetic reference system used by GPS, including a reference ellipsoid and coordinate frame. Converting to the British National Grid requires a projection and datum transformation.
